**Mechanical Engineering Graduate \| CAE • Explicit Dynamics • Occupant Biomechanics • Model Validation**
MASc graduate in Mechanical and Mechatronics Engineering with experience in LS-DYNA, FE model validation, occupant safety, DOE, automation, and experimental correlation.

*Last updated: 13 September 2026*

I am a recent mechanical engineering graduate specializing in **nonlinear FEA, explicit dynamics, model validation, and injury biomechanics**. During my MASc at the University of Waterloo, I used LS-DYNA, physical sled test data, and statistical analysis to study frontal impact occupant safety.
I enjoy work that connects **simulation, physical behavior, quantitative validation, and practical design decisions**. My experience also includes mechanical design, electromechanical prototyping, biomedical projects, and engineering documentation.

- **Engineering background:** MASc in Mechanical and Mechatronics Engineering, completed July 2026; BASc in Mechanical Engineering, Biomedical Option
- **Simulation & CAE:** LS-DYNA, nonlinear FEA, explicit dynamics, material response, contact, and boundary conditions
- **Validation & analysis:** physical test correlation, ISO 18571, DOE, ANOVA, MATLAB, JMP, and Excel
- **Design & prototyping:** SolidWorks, Onshape, sensors, Arduino, controls, and experimental testing
- **Technical communication:** thesis, conference work, sponsor presentations, reports, SOPs, and collaborative design

---

### Graduate Research
[**THOR-5F Rear Seat Occupant Safety Research**](/projects/thor-5f/)
- Validated two LS-DYNA rear seat bench models against physical test data.
- Ran **104 simulations** to evaluate how shoulder and lap belt anchor positions affected occupant response.
- **Validation basis:** Each bench achieved an average ISO 18571 rating of **0.71** across ten signals, corresponding to a **Fair** grade. Signal-level and kinematic agreement supported comparative sensitivity analysis, while local limitations were carried into the interpretation.
- Shoulder anchor peak chest deflection ranged from **42 to 63 mm** in the Rigid Bench and **35.0 to 49.6 mm** in the Semi-Rigid Bench. In the SAE coordinate system used for the study, rearward is XMIN and inboard is YMAX. The lowest rearward/inboard configurations produced **42 mm** and **35.0 mm**, respectively, which were **17% and 16% below** their bench study averages.

title: THOR-5F Rear Seat Occupant Safety Research

blocks.text:
**Validated THOR-5F simulation → quantified restraint-geometry effects**
For my MASc research, I developed two LS-DYNA rear seat bench models, compared the THOR-5F response with physical sled test data, and completed 104 physically feasible DOE runs across four shoulder and lap belt anchor studies. I combined kinematic comparisons, ISO 18571, and least-squares effects models while carrying test and model limitations into the conclusions.

### Scope
- **104** physically feasible anchor position simulations
- **4** three-factor, three-level full-factorial studies
- **2** rear seat bench configurations with physical benchmarks
- **10** quantitative signals in each validation assessment
- **0.71** average ISO 18571 rating in each bench (**Fair**)
- Shoulder anchor peak chest deflection ranged from **42 to 63 mm** in the Rigid Bench and **35.0 to 49.6 mm** in the Semi-Rigid Bench; the lowest rearward/inboard configurations were **17% and 16% below** their respective bench study averages
- Repeated belt fitting workflow reduced from **seven manual setup steps to four** using editable LS-PrePost command files
- **Tools:** LS-DYNA, LS-PrePost, MATLAB, JMP, Excel

Rear seat occupant safety remains a concern in frontal impacts, particularly for small-stature female occupants and regarding thoracic injury. The THOR-5F was developed with updated anthropometry and four chest deflection sensors, creating a stronger tool for studying how restraint geometry affects localized chest loading.
The seat belt anchor position changes the load path between the restraint and the occupant. It can alter when the belt engages, where load is transferred, how the torso and pelvis move, and how much the chest deforms.
Before comparing anchor locations, I first needed to answer a more fundamental question: **Did the FE model reproduce the relevant physical response well enough to support a comparative design study?**

This project was the focus of my MASc research. The contribution statement for the associated conference paper lists my roles as **manuscript writing, methodology, simulations, data analysis, and visualization**. My technical work included:
- Developing the rigid and simplified semi-rigid LS-DYNA bench models from project-provided and published geometry, loading, and material inputs.
- Positioning the THOR-5F FE model to measured or published test postures using landmark data, 3D comparisons, and marionette positioning pre-simulations.
- Implementing and calibrating the restraint models, including the semi-rigid 4-point, 2-belt benchmark and the 3-point configuration used for the comparative DOE.
- Developing reusable LS-PrePost scripting and QA steps for repetitive belt fitting and model preparation.
- Running and troubleshooting the simulations, then extracting, filtering, and comparing equivalent model and test signals.
- Quantifying model-to-test agreement with ISO 18571 and supplementing the ratings with frame-by-frame kinematic assessment.
- Designing and analyzing the four anchor position studies using least-squares regression, interaction terms, and ANOVA in JMP.
- Interpreting and communicating the work through my thesis, conference paper, and presentation, and sponsor-facing technical updates.
The physical Rigid Bench tests were conducted by Transport Canada/PMG Technologies; the Semi-Rigid Bench test data were sourced from published literature, and the base THOR-5F FE model was commercially supplied. My contribution was developing the CAE environments and applying, validating, and using the occupant model to answer the questions about restraint geometry.

These specifications are limited to information disclosed in my released thesis. THOR-5F element counts, mesh density, element formulations, material definitions, and a total assembly element count are excluded because the dummy model is a licensed commercial model covered by confidentiality restrictions.
Item Published specification
Solver LS-DYNA R12.2.1, MPP, single precision
Pre-processorLS-PrePost V4.10; seat belt routing
Compute system Nibi cluster, 32 cores, Intel 6972P at 2.4 GHz, 348 MB cache
Simulation termination 225 ms total: 100 ms of belt slack removal followed by the first 125 ms of the crash pulse
Rigid Bench input 23 g peak pulse, averaged from three Transport Canada and PMG Technologies sled pulses using ARCGen
Semi-Rigid Bench input 9 g peak pulse
Contact friction 0.28 for occupant-to-bench contact and 0.30 for occupant-to-belt contact, both taken from the ENOP model
Belt modeling Two-dimensional elements for the webbing; one-dimensional elements connecting the webbing to sliprings and anchors
Bench mechanisms Beam elements for anchor revolute joints; discrete elements in the Semi-Rigid Bench
Constrained components The seat pan and anti-submarining pan were constrained from deforming
Signal processing SAE J211 recommended filters were applied to corresponding model and test channels
Numerical stability The belt fitting and slack removal simulations remained numerically stable, with no error terminations or instabilities.

1. **Build the benchmark environments.** Modeled a 23 g Rigid Bench and compared it with three matched TC/PMG sled tests. Built a simplified Semi-Rigid Bench and assessed the THOR-5F with a 4-point, 2-belt system against two published 9 g tests.
2. **Match initial conditions.** Reproduced occupant posture, belt position, bench geometry, crash pulse, contacts, constraints, and output requests before solving.
3. **Implement and calibrate the restraints.** Routed the belts in LS-PrePost, removed measured slack, represented retractor behavior, and calibrated otherwise unmodeled compliance in the semi-rigid benchmark.
4. **Standardize repeated work.** Used editable LS-PrePost command files and repeatable QA checks to improve consistency during belt fitting and model preparation.
5. **Compare equivalent evidence.** Processed ten quantitative signals: head resultant acceleration, four chest deflections, pelvis resultant acceleration, left and right iliac forces, and shoulder and lap belt loads. Kinematic snapshots were assessed separately for occupant motion and belt interaction.
6. **Validate quantitatively.** Compared waveform timing, magnitude, and shape and calculated ISO 18571 ratings rather than relying only on visual agreement.
7. **Prepare the comparative study.** Converted the semi-rigid model to a representative 3-point belt configuration and used the validated models to investigate anchor position sensitivity.

For each bench, the average ISO 18571 rating across the ten quantitative signals was **0.71**, corresponding to a **Fair** grade. Together with the signal-level and kinematic agreement during the primary loading phase, this supported using the models for a comparative sensitivity study rather than claiming full predictive validation. Belt loads and pelvis acceleration received Good ratings in both benches; the weakest agreement occurred in the rigid bench left-lower chest response and the semi-rigid iliac force signals.

Additionally,  I reviewed the signal-level ratings, time histories, belt motion, and occupant kinematics before deciding which responses could support the anchor study. This process made validation an engineering decision process rather than a single-number claim.
### Validation Interpretation
- In the Rigid Bench, belt loads and pelvis acceleration matched well, but the FE model developed less torso Z-rotation and did not reproduce the physical belt migration toward the shoulder edge. This contributed to differences in head acceleration and left lower-chest flexion.
- In the Semi-Rigid Bench, forward motion and the primary restraint-loading phase were reproduced well after accounting for unmodeled belt system compliance; iliac force signals remained a limitation.
- The physical right-lower chest sensor bottomed out in both benchmark datasets, creating a plateau that was not found in the FE model.
- The FE model did not reproduce these differences, which were carried into the DOE interpretation rather than being hidden by the overall 0.71 ratings.

### Kinematic Comparison
I used time-aligned snapshots with the response histories to compare posture, forward excursion, pitch, torso rotation, and belt path through the event. The rigid benchmark exposed reduced torso rotation and different belt migration in the FE model, while the semi-rigid benchmark showed similar forward motion with smaller late differences in pitch and arm extension.

**Coordinate convention:** Anchor locations use the SAE coordinate system. +X is forward, +Y is toward the right side of the bench, and +Z is downward. The origin is at the mid-width of the raised platform's rear edge, and the Rearward locations are XMIN, and the inboard locations are YMAX.
After validation, I created four three-factor, three-level full-factorial studies: separate investigations of shoulder and lap belt anchors in the Rigid and Semi-Rigid Benches. The minimum midpoint and maximum X/Y/Z levels were derived from a published survey of 24 vehicle rear seat geometries.

- Ran **27 shoulder anchor cases per bench** and **25 physically feasible lap anchor cases per bench**, for **104 LS-DYNA simulations** in total.
- Measured the peak at each of the four chest sensors, the overall peak chest deflection, and the peak pelvis resultant acceleration.
- Screened configurations with non-characteristic belt migration or submarining from the effects analysis; two lap anchor locations per bench could not be simulated because the anchors intersected the pelvis.
- Used a first-order **least-squares regression model with main and interaction terms**, followed by ANOVA in JMP, to analyze the resulting unbalanced datasets.
- Compared the same design space across both benches to distinguish geometry effects from bench-dependent kinematics.
This approach identified not only **which** response changed, but also **which variables, interactions, and kinematic modes were driving it**.

### From Simulation to Effect
Each factor was coded as minimum (-1), midpoint (0), or maximum (+1). A main effect was the estimated difference between the average responses at the maximum and minimum levels.
The fitted regression model included X, Y, Z, XY, XZ, YZ, and XYZ terms, allowing effects to be estimated consistently despite screened or infeasible configurations.

Question Finding
Was the model suitable for comparative study? Each bench achieved an average ISO 18571 rating of 0.71 across ten quantitative signals, providing a transparent basis for comparative sensitivity analysis.
What most affected chest response? Shoulder anchor fore/aft and lateral position had the largest chest deflection effects in both benches. In the Rigid Bench, peak chest deflection ranged from 42 to 63 mm, with a study average of 51 mm and 50.6 mm at midpoint Position 14. Position 7 produced the lowest response, 17% below the study average, while Position 19 produced the highest response, 24% above the study average. In the Semi-Rigid Bench, peak chest deflection ranged from 35.0 to 49.6 mm, with a study average of 41.7 mm and 42.0 mm at midpoint Position 14. Position 8 produced the lowest response, 16% below the study average, while Position 22 produced the highest response, 19% above the study average. The study average was retained because the main-effect method compares average responses across factor levels; in both benches, the midpoint response was close to that average.
What most affected pelvic response? Lap anchor position affected pelvis acceleration more strongly than shoulder anchor position. In the Rigid Bench lap anchor study, peak pelvis resultant acceleration ranged from 30.8 to 54.8 g, with a study average of 43.6 g and a midpoint response of 42.3 g. The average was therefore 1.3 g higher than the midpoint. Rearward, upward, and inboard locations were associated with lower responses after configurations showing submarining or near-submarining were excluded from the interpretation. In the Semi-Rigid Bench, the response was dominated by lateral position and by a coupled lateral-vertical interaction.
What improved the workflow? LS-PrePost scripting reduced repetitive manual setup and improved consistency across the simulation matrix.

- **Rearward shoulder anchors** engaged the torso earlier, reducing forward excursion and making load transfer more gradual.
- **Inboard shoulder anchors** improved contact with the shoulder and reduced loading on the chest, but extreme inboard routing introduced a belt-to-neck tradeoff.
- **Lap anchor effects were more configuration-dependent.** The rigid bench primarily produced forward motion; the semi-rigid footrest and rotating seat pan introduced coupled forward/downward motion and stronger interaction effects.
- The favorable shoulder anchor region remained within the evaluated FMVSS/CMVSS 210 fore/aft and vertical range, but the important lateral effect is not represented by that range. Regulatory placement alone therefore does not guarantee an effective belt fit for a small-stature occupant.
**Interpretation boundary:** These results identify simulated sensitivities within the evaluated design space. Some positions represented fleet extremes or produced non-characteristic restraint behavior. The findings are not, by themselves, a production restraint system recommendation, and the preliminary injury-risk estimates were intentionally omitted from this public summary.

- MASc thesis: *Assessment of Seat Belt Anchor Position on Rear Seat Occupant Kinematics in Frontal Impact Using a Validated THOR-5F Finite Element Model*
- [Conference paper](https://ibrc.osu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Thangarajah-20th-IBS-Paper.pdf) and presentation at the **20th Injury Biomechanics Symposium, The Ohio State University**
- Contributions to six sponsor-facing technical presentations and written research deliverables

- [Quantitative FE Model Validation | ISO 18571](/projects/fe-validation/): response channels, correlation method, and validation reasoning
- [Seat Belt Anchor DOE & Statistical Analysis](/projects/seat-belt-doe/): factor design, main effects, interactions, and engineering interpretation
- [LS-PrePost Automation for Simulation Setup](/projects/ls-prepost-automation/): scripting and repeatable preprocessing

**Explicit dynamics • occupant biomechanics • restraint system mechanics • model validation • physical test correlation • DOE • statistical interpretation • CAE automation • technical communication**
**External-sharing boundary:** This page includes methods and results already disclosed through public academic work. Proprietary model data, raw test files, partner-specific inputs, and restricted screenshots are intentionally omitted.
**Focus:** Establish model credibility before using simulation to compare restraint designs.

I built and calibrated both LS-DYNA benchmark environments, matched the occupant posture and restraint setup, processed the comparison channels, calculated ISO 18571 ratings, and used the quantitative and kinematic evidence to decide which responses could support the anchor position study. Transport Canada and PMG Technologies conducted the rigid bench tests; the semi-rigid data came from published sled tests.

A crash animation can look plausible while still missing important timing, load path, or local response behavior. I therefore treated validation as a combination of quantitative signal correlation and qualitative kinematic assessment.

Configuration Benchmark Purpose
Rigid Bench Three matched TC/PMG sled tests with a 23 g frontal pulse and 3-point belt Validate the model in a controlled, repeatable environment
Semi-Rigid Bench Two published 9 g tests using a pivoting seat and 4-point, 2-belt system Assess response with seat pan rotation and footrest interaction
The validated semi-rigid model was subsequently converted to a representative 3-point belt configuration for comparison with the Rigid Bench in the anchor position study. ### Reconstructing the Initial Position

The same ten response types were evaluated in each bench:
- Head resultant acceleration
- Four IR-TRACC chest deflections: left/right and upper/lower
- Pelvis resultant acceleration
- Left and right iliac forces
- Shoulder belt load
- Lap belt load

Occupant posture, forward excursion, torso rotation, pitch, and belt migration were evaluated separately through synchronized images; torso rotation was not one of the ten ISO-scored signals.

1. Reproduced the relevant bench geometry, loading, restraints, and initial THOR-5F position.
2. Routed and checked the belts and matched the available initial belt position and tension measurements.
3. Applied SAE J211 filtering to corresponding model and test responses.
4. Compared signal timing, magnitude, shape, and local discrepancies.
5. Calculated ISO 18571 ratings for each signal and averaged across the physical test repeats.
6. Used kinematic images to explain differences that a waveform score alone could not identify.

### Selected Absolute Differences The ISO 18571 ratings were interpreted alongside the magnitude and timing differences in the response histories: - Rigid Bench, final validated model: Iliac load cell peaks were approximately 1 kN lower than the physical test responses. - Semi-Rigid Bench, initial assessment with immediate retractor locking, before compliance calibration: Belt loads peaked approximately 10 ms earlier than the physical tests and were approximately 0.5 kN (15%) lower in the model. - Semi-Rigid Bench, initial assessment with immediate retractor locking, before compliance calibration: Resultant pelvis acceleration peaked 10 ms (13%) earlier and underpredicted the peak magnitude by more than 5 g (24%). These differences were retained as validation limitations rather than being obscured by the overall 0.71 average rating.
Bench Average ISO 18571 rating Strongest agreement Important limitation
Rigid 0.71 (Fair) Pelvis acceleration and shoulder and lap belt loads (Good) Left-lower chest response; reduced torso Z-rotation and different belt migration
Semi-Rigid 0.71 (Fair) Head and pelvis acceleration and shoulder and lap belt loads (Good) Iliac force signals; simplified restraint system compliance

- In the Rigid Bench, the model matched early forward motion and peak restraint timing, but the physical ATD rotated farther, and the belt migrated toward the shoulder edge. The model's reduced rotation contributed to the head and left-lower chest differences.
- In the Semi-Rigid Bench, the primary loading phase and forward motion compared well after belt system compliance was calibrated. Minor late differences in pitch and arm extension occurred after maximum excursion.
- The physical right-lower chest sensor bottomed out in both benchmark datasets, producing a plateau that the FE model did not reproduce.
- Iliac force disagreement was treated as a sensor/load path limitation even when lap belt load and pelvis acceleration matched well.
### Kinematic Evidence

I compared the FE time sequences with the physical benchmarks alongside the response histories. In the TC/PMG Rigid Bench tests, the physical ATD developed greater torso rotation, and the shoulder belt migrated farther toward the shoulder edge than in the model. In the Semi-Rigid Bench comparison, the model reproduced the primary forward motion and restraint-loading phase, with smaller late differences in pitch and arm extension relative to the physical test response reported by Richard et al. (2022). The physical imagery is not reproduced here.

The models were sufficiently representative for a **comparative anchor position sensitivity study**, particularly for chest deflection, pelvis acceleration, belt loading, and overall occupant motion. The 0.71 averages were not treated as blanket validation of every local signal.

**Public-sharing boundary:** This summary uses methods and results disclosed in the thesis. Raw test files, proprietary model inputs, and restricted partner material are excluded.

title: Seat Belt Anchor DOE & Statistical Analysis

blocks.text: **Goal:** Convert a large restraint-geometry design space into defensible, physically interpreted trends.

I defined the four DOE matrices, prepared and completed the 104 LS-DYNA cases, screened non-characteristic restraint responses, fitted the least-squares effects models in JMP, and interpreted the statistics together with the occupant kinematics.
How do fore/aft, lateral, and vertical shoulder and lap belt anchor positions affect THOR-5F chest deformation and pelvis response, and which effects change when the seat environment changes?

**Coordinate convention:** Anchor locations use the SAE coordinate system. +X is forward, +Y is toward the right side of the bench and +Z is downward. The origin is at the mid-width of the raised platform rear edge. Rearward locations are XMIN, and inboard locations are YMAX. Four separate three-factor, three-level full-factorial studies were defined: shoulder and lap anchors in both the Rigid and Semi-Rigid Benches.
Study element Definition
Factors Anchor X (fore/aft), Y (lateral), and Z (vertical) position
Levels Minimum (-1), midpoint (0), and maximum (+1)
Design range Published measurements from 24 vehicle rear seat geometries
Shoulder anchor runs 27 per bench; lap anchors held at midpoint
Lap anchor runs 25 physically feasible per bench; shoulder anchor held at midpoint
Solver and compute LS-DYNA v12.2.1, MPP, single precision; approximately 1.5 hours per simulation
Total 104 completed LS-DYNA simulations

- Peak deflection from each of the four chest sensors
- Overall peak chest deflection, defined as the maximum of the four sensors
- Peak pelvis resultant acceleration

Two lap anchor locations per bench could not be simulated because the nominal anchor points intersected the THOR-5F pelvis. Additional results were screened from the effects analysis when the restraint response was non-characteristic, including shoulder belt migration from the torso or submarining at high lap belt positions.
The remaining data formed unbalanced datasets. I fitted a first-order least-squares model containing **X, Y, Z, XY, XZ, YZ, and XYZ** terms, then used ANOVA in JMP to evaluate effects at the 0.05 significance level. The model estimated the underlying trends at screened configurations while avoiding a higher-order fit that would overfit the reduced samples.
A main effect was defined as the estimated difference between the average response at a factor's maximum and minimum levels. Interaction terms captured cases where the effect of one direction depended on another anchor coordinate.

### From Simulation Output to a Design Trend
For each configuration, I extracted the peak response, grouped the results by coded factor level, and used the fitted model to estimate main and interaction effects. I then returned to the animations and belt paths to explain why statistically important changes occurred.

### Absolute Response Summary
Anchor study Peak chest deflection Peak pelvis resultant acceleration Additional result
Shoulder anchor, Rigid Bench 42 to 63 mm; 51 mm average; Position 14 midpoint at 50.6 mm; Position 7 was 17% below average; Position 19 was 24% above average 36.4 to 49.0 g; 42.6 g average Chest deflection regression R² = 0.92
Lap anchor, Rigid Bench 44.3 to 53.1 mm; 49.2 mm average; Position 5 was 10% below average 30.8 to 54.8 g; 43.6 g average; 42.3 g midpoint The average pelvis response was 1.3 g higher than the midpoint
Shoulder anchor, Semi-Rigid Bench 35.0 to 49.6 mm; 41.7 mm average; Position 14 midpoint at 42.0 mm; Position 8 was 16% below average; Position 22 was 19% above average 34.8 to 45.6 g; 39.8 g average; 37.6 g midpoint The midpoint chest response was close to the study average
Lap anchor, Semi-Rigid Bench 40.3 to 44.6 mm; 42.4 mm average; 42.0 mm midpoint; Position 2 was 5% above average Not included Chest response varied over a comparatively narrow range
For rigid bench shoulder anchor chest deflection, the fitted regression produced R² = 0.92. Moving X from minimum to maximum increased the estimated response by 9.5 mm. Moving Y from minimum to maximum reduced it by 6.5 mm, while moving Z from minimum to maximum reduced it by 4.5 mm. The XZ interaction contributed an estimated effect of -3.16 mm, showing that the vertical effect depended on the fore/aft position.
Question Result
What controlled peak chest deflection? Shoulder anchor X and Y position were the dominant effects in both benches. Peak chest deflection ranged from 42 to 63 mm in the Rigid Bench and 35.0 to 49.6 mm in the Semi-Rigid Bench. The lowest rearward/inboard configurations produced 42 mm and 35.0 mm, respectively, which were 17% and 16% below their bench study averages. The study average was retained because the main-effect method compares average responses across factor levels; the midpoint was close to that average in both benches (50.6 mm versus 51.0 mm for the Rigid Bench, and 42.0 mm versus 41.7 mm for the Semi-Rigid Bench).
How did vertical shoulder position contribute? Moving the shoulder anchor downward, from ZMIN to ZMAX in the SAE coordinate system, produced a smaller estimated reduction in chest deflection. However, the lowest observed rigid bench configuration was at ZMIN because the XZ interaction weakened the vertical effect at XMIN. The best observed configuration was therefore not obtained by simply combining the individually favorable main-effect levels.
How important were lap anchors to chest response? They had a smaller overall effect than shoulder anchors and produced more bench-dependent interactions.
What controlled pelvis acceleration? Lap anchor position had the larger influence because the lap belt directly loaded the pelvis.
What occurred in the Rigid Bench? Rearward, upward, and inboard lap anchor trends reduced pelvis acceleration after excluding submarining or near-submarining interpretations.
What occurred in the Semi-Rigid Bench? Lateral position and the lateral/vertical interaction were significant; the interaction was approximately twice the lateral main effect, showing strong coupling with seat pan motion.

- Rearward shoulder anchors engaged the torso earlier, reducing excursion and making restraint loading more gradual.
- Inboard shoulder anchors transferred more load through the shoulder rather than the chest, but extreme inboard routing increased the risk of belt-to-neck contact.
- The Rigid Bench primarily allowed forward occupant motion and therefore depended more strongly on belt geometry.
- The Semi-Rigid Bench added footrest support and coupled forward/downward motion from the rotating seat pan, producing more complex lap anchor interactions.

Most favorable shoulder anchor trends remained inside the evaluated FMVSS/CMVSS 210 fore/aft and vertical range. However, lateral position, which strongly affected chest response and belt fit, is not represented by that range. Compliance with an anchor position envelope alone does not demonstrate an optimal fit for a small-stature occupant.
These findings are comparative sensitivities within the simulated range, not a production restraint specification. Some factor combinations represented fleet extremes, the regression assumed smooth first-order behavior, and shoulder/lap anchor interactions were not studied simultaneously.
**Public-sharing boundary:** This page includes only methods and results disclosed in my thesis. Raw test data, proprietary model inputs, and restricted partner material are excluded.
**Impact:** Standardized the repeated belt fitting workflow with editable LS-PrePost command files, reducing manual setup from seven steps to four while improving consistency across the DOE.

The scientific study required 104 physically feasible anchor position simulations. Each geometry change required belt routing, slack removal, interference checks, and model QA. Repeating those steps entirely by hand created a significant preprocessing bottleneck and increased the chance of inconsistent setup.

I used editable LS-PrePost command files (`.cfile`) to automate repeatable belt fitting operations. For each anchor configuration, I first applied the new anchor coordinates, updated the configuration-specific node identifiers in the command file, and ran the same fitting sequence for both the shoulder and lap portions of the belt. I retained manual engineering checks for geometry and contact quality.

1. Applied the shoulder or lap anchor coordinates for the new DOE configuration.
2. Updated the configuration-specific node identifiers in the LS-PrePost command file.
3. Ran the `.cfile` sequence to fit both the shoulder and lap portions of the belt.
4. Accepted the generated quadrilateral belt geometry into the model.
5. Inspected the routed belt for warped elements, jacket interference, D-ring interaction, and appropriate belt conformity.
6. Corrected any geometry or contact issues before releasing the model for solution.

```plain text
$# Sanitised LS-PrePost command-file structure
beltfit fitbelt ... <configuration-specific node identifiers> ...
beltfit accept <belt part identifiers> quad
```
This excerpt shows the command mechanism without exposing project node or part identifiers. Anchor coordinates were applied before running the file; the identifiers were then edited for each configuration.

The command-file workflow reduced the repeated belt fitting sequence from seven manual steps to four: opening the file, generating the shoulder belt fit, generating the lap belt fit, and running the command file. The command file automated steps I had previously done manually, including renaming and saving each belt part, deleting the jacket used during fitting, and saving the completed belt file. Elapsed setup time was not measured.

- More consistent preprocessing across a large DOE
- Less repetitive manual work
- Reduced opportunity for avoidable setup errors
- Faster iteration when a model required correction
- Clear separation between scripted operations and engineering judgment

**LS-PrePost 4.10 • LS-DYNA model preparation • restraint system modeling • LS-PrePost command-file scripting • model QA**

**Scope note:** The automation supported the research workflow; the thesis's primary scientific contribution remained model validation and the anchor position sensitivity analysis.

title: Cervical Fracture Mechanics in Football Impact

blocks.text:
**Helmeted head-first impact simulation - comparing standardized injury metrics with explicit vertebral failure**
I independently investigated how impact velocity and neck orientation influenced cervical loading and predicted fracture during head-first football impacts. Using LS-DYNA, I simulated five configurations with Hybrid III and GHBMC models, compared predicted peak forces and injury locations with published cadaveric studies, and evaluated whether the Neck Injury Criterion captured the model-predicted fracture response.

Head-first football impacts can align the cervical spine with the impact load and create a high risk of axial-compression injury. I investigated two related questions: **How do velocity and impact angle change the cervical response, and how does an ATD-based injury metric compare with explicit fracture predicted by a human body model?**

I completed this project independently. I:
- Integrated a helmeted Hybrid III head-and-neck model with a full-body Hybrid III model and defined the tied interface.
- Prepared the helmeted 50th-percentile male GHBMC model and its existing cortical- and cancellous-bone failure definitions.
- Created the rigid impact plate, contacts, initial conditions, and five impact configurations in LS-DYNA.
- Extracted neck section forces and moments, calculated maximum Nij, inspected predicted vertebral failure, and compared the results with published cadaveric studies.

1. **Build the models.** Prepared helmeted Hybrid III and GHBMC full-body models and a 5 mm-mesh rigid steel impact plate.
2. **Define the matrix.** Simulated perpendicular impacts at 3.4, 4.1, and 7.0 m/s, plus -15 degree and +30 degree plate orientations at 3.4 m/s.
3. **Run and post-process.** Solved the five configurations in LS-DYNA 7.1.2 and extracted neck section forces and moments.
4. **Interpret the response.** Calculated Nij for both models, identified primary GHBMC fracture locations from element failure, and compared GHBMC neck forces with experimental literature.

Configuration Hybrid III max Nij GHBMC max Nij Primary GHBMC fracture
3.4 m/s, 0 degrees 2.01 0.86 C2
4.1 m/s, 0 degrees 2.34 0.87 C1-C3
7.0 m/s, 0 degrees 3.71 3.47 C1-C3
3.4 m/s, +30 degrees 1.57 0.72 C1
3.4 m/s, -15 degrees 1.85 0.64 C2-C3
- The GHBMC predicted cervical fracture in **all five configurations**, while its Nij exceeded 1 only in the 7.0 m/s case. - GHBMC peak neck forces of **2.26 kN at 3.4 m/s** and **2.34 kN at 4.1 m/s** fell within the ranges reported by two cadaveric studies. - Increasing perpendicular impact speed increased fracture extent. The +30 degree case produced the least visible damage. - The simulations predicted primarily upper-cervical damage at C1-C3, whereas one comparison study reported lower-cervical C5-C6 fractures. ### Predicted Fracture Progression

Hybrid III and GHBMC answered different questions. The Hybrid III provided the force and moment outputs used for standardized Nij assessment, while the GHBMC represented anatomical structure and predicted local bone failure. The mismatch between sub-threshold GHBMC Nij values and predicted fracture in four cases showed why an ATD-derived scalar metric should not be treated as a direct fracture predictor in a human body model.

This project followed an injury-mechanism analysis workflow relevant to forensic biomechanics: defining a loading scenario, testing sensitivity to impact conditions and posture, comparing model response with published injury-tolerance data, and identifying where a standard injury criterion did not reproduce the simulated outcome. This was a controlled individual course study, not a reconstruction of a real incident.

- The impact-plate angle was varied instead of repositioning and preloading the cervical spine.
- The rigid plate and helmet simplified the compliant player-to-player impact environment.
- Both models represented a 50th-percentile male rather than NFL player anthropometry; active muscle response was not included.
- The upper-cervical fracture locations differed from one experimental dataset, limiting direct validation of injury location.

**LS-DYNA explicit dynamics \| Hybrid III and GHBMC modeling \| injury-criterion interpretation \| cervical fracture mechanics \| simulation post-processing \| literature comparison**

title: Soft Distensible Bladder Test Platform - UBC Capstone

blocks.text:
**Four-person UBC Mechanical Engineering capstone for Echoscope**
We designed and built a benchtop platform that reproduced bladder filling, ureteric jetting, external pressurization, and voiding so the client could test an ultrasound-based bladder-monitoring device. The completed system met the main quantitative requirements and supported repeatable pressure and volume measurements.

The client needed a physical bladder model that could behave more like a real, distensible bladder than a rigid container. The platform also needed to control filling and jetting, apply external pressure during voiding, and record the pressure-volume response.

**Academic capstone, September 2022 to April 2023:** This was a four-person MECH 45X project at UBC. The integrated platform, bladder phantom, pressure chamber, and client validation were team deliverables. My primary ownership was the sensing, control, and data acquisition system.

**R&D Engineer, Echoscope \| Part-time and remote \| 10 May to 8 September 2023**
Following the capstone, I continued working with Echoscope as a part-time remote R&D Engineer. I authored five manufacturing and verification procedures covering PCB assembly, wiring, software setup, perfboard software, and PCB functionality testing. All five procedures were delivered to the client, translating prototype knowledge into repeatable build and verification documentation.

My main responsibility was the sensing and control system, with additional work across concept development, phantom testing, chamber construction, and final integration. I:
- Worked with the client to translate the initial need into engineering requirements and evaluation criteria.
- Generated and evaluated concepts, including pump and pressurization approaches, using structured concept-selection methods.
- Cast silicone bladder prototypes in 3D-printed molds, compared wall thickness and material through pressure-volume testing, and helped revise the process to address trapped air, leakage, and difficult demolding.
- Characterized the peristaltic pump, selected the motor driver, and developed Arduino PWM control.
- Replaced the original sensing approach with an analog pressure sensor, built a three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier, and calibrated the sensor against a reference device.
- Developed the MATLAB interface used to control filling and ureteric-jet parameters, display pressure-time and pressure-volume curves, and record the test data.
- Helped machine, seal, troubleshoot, and validate the plexiglass pressure chamber before integrating the full system.

blocks.title: Test Method Development and Verification Workflow

blocks.text:
1. **Define requirements and acceptance criteria.** Converted the client's needs into measurable targets for flow, pressure-volume accuracy, voiding pressure, chamber size, and usability.
2. **Develop the test specimen.** Tested elastomers and wall thicknesses, refined the silicone molding process, and selected Ecoflex 00-10.
3. **Build the controlled test method.** Integrated the phantom with a peristaltic filling pump, pressure chamber, pressure sensor, and manually controlled outlet.
4. **Automate control and data acquisition.** Connected the pump and sensor through Arduino hardware and a MATLAB interface that controlled the test inputs, displayed live response curves, and recorded results.
5. **Verify against the criteria.** Compared the pressure-volume response with the target curve, checked chamber pressurization, and completed a client usability assessment.

Subsystem Final Design
Bladder phantom Ecoflex 00-10 silicone, manufactured as two molded halves and sealed together
Fluid control Peristaltic pump with a maximum measured flow rate of 19 mL/s and adjustable ureteric-jet parameters
Pressure chamber 30 x 30 x 30 cm plexiglass enclosure with a neoprene gasket, sealed joints, and an airtight access zipper
Pressure measurement Analog pressure sensor with a calibrated three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier
Control and logging Arduino, motor driver, and MATLAB interface for pump control, live plots, and data recording

Requirement Target Achieved Result
Filling flow rate At least 12 mL/s Up to 19 mL/s Met
Pressure-volume curve error No more than 60% 24.3% Met
Internal pressure during voiding 4.4 to 4.9 kPa 4.75 kPa maximum Met
Pressure chamber volume No more than 54,000 cm³ 27,000 cm³ Met
- The pressure chamber produced and maintained approximately **2.2 kPa**, with a **13.8 second** pressure ramp. - The client rated the system **5/5 for timing**, **5/5 for overall function**, **4.5/5 for ease of use**, and **3/5 for aesthetics**.

- **Pressure sensing:** Switching from the original sensor setup to an analog sensor allowed one Arduino to read pressure and control the pump. The instrumentation amplifier improved the usable measurement range.
- **Chamber sealing:** Leakage around the lid limited early pressure tests. A rubber gasket, improved caulking, mechanical fastening, and an airtight zipper allowed the final chamber to hold pressure.
- **Material selection:** The team compared multiple materials and thicknesses instead of choosing the phantom material from stiffness alone. Ecoflex 00-10 produced the best overall pressure-volume match.
- **Molding process:** Early casts exposed trapped air, leakage, and difficult demolding. Revising the molds and handling steps improved the repeatability of the silicone prototypes.

The final prototype still used manual outlet control and did not directly measure voiding volume. The pumps and electrical hardware also needed a dedicated enclosure. Recommended next steps included closed-loop pump control, an automated outlet valve, a flow sensor, and improved packaging.

**Client-focused product development, requirements definition, silicone molding, prototyping, pressure sensor calibration, analog circuits, Arduino control, MATLAB interface development, machining, system integration, PCB documentation, and verification testing**

title: Seat Foam Effects on Rear Impact Injury Response

blocks.text:
**Rear impact LS-DYNA study - connecting seat foam material response to occupant head and neck injury metrics**
For this individual ME 725 course project, I compared five polyurethane seat foam models in a Hybrid III rear impact sled model at 27 and 57 km/h. The JC80 foam produced the lowest HIC15 at both severities, while the foam ranking for Nij changed with impact severity.

Seatback and head restraint foams absorb energy and affect the timing of occupant loading in a rear impact. I investigated: **How much do different seat foam material responses affect head and neck injury metrics, and are those effects consistent across crash severity?**

I completed this as an individual course project, building on an existing Hybrid III seat model and occupant-settling setup. I:
- Created single-element LS-DYNA compression models to check the material response against available stress-strain data.
- Implemented and compared five `*MAT_LOW_DENSITY_FOAM` definitions in the head restraint and seatback of a detailed 2018 Honda Odyssey rear seat model.
- Ran five foam configurations at each of two rear impact pulses, giving **10 sled simulations**.
- Extracted head-head-restraint contact force, head acceleration, and upper neck force and moment histories.
- Calculated and compared **HIC15 and Nij** across the complete simulation matrix.

1. **Define the materials.** Compared five polyurethane foam responses using the LS-DYNA low-density foam material model.
2. **Check the input response.** Compressed a 1 x 1 x 1 mm solid element at 1 mm/s and compared the calculated stress-strain response with the available input curves.
3. **Integrate the foams.** Updated the head restraint and seatback material definitions in the detailed seat model while keeping the remaining setup consistent.
4. **Settle and load the occupant.** Used the existing positioning procedure, gravity settling, and NHTSA rear impact pulses at 27 and 57 km/h.
5. **Post-process the response.** Compared contact forces, upper neck force and moment, HIC15, and maximum Nij.

The four non-default foam models reproduced their available input stress-strain behavior in the single-element checks. The default NHTSA foam could not be checked the same way because its original experimental curve was not provided.

Foam HIC15 - 57 km/h HIC15 - 27 km/h Nij - 57 km/h Nij - 27 km/h
JC120 562.2 223.8 2.12 0.770
JC80 513.1 210.6 2.49 0.616
Campbell Foam 2 565.1 242.8 1.63 0.914
Campbell Foam 4 628.0 262.1 2.70 0.931
NHTSA default 574.6 231.9 2.81 1.05
- All simulated HIC15 values remained below **700** at both impact severities. - JC80 produced the lowest HIC15 in both cases. Its value was **18.3% lower at 57 km/h** and **19.6% lower at 27 km/h** than Campbell Foam 4, which produced the highest HIC15 in both cases. - At 57 km/h, every foam produced a maximum Nij above **1.0**; Campbell Foam 2 produced the lowest value at **1.63**. - At 27 km/h, four foam alternatives remained below Nij = 1.0, while the default NHTSA foam reached **1.05**. JC80 produced the lowest value at **0.616**. - The force and moment histories were broadly similar between foams, and the Nij ranking changed with crash severity.

Within this model, the lower-modulus JC80 foam was associated with lower head injury response at both speeds. The neck response was less consistent: the foam producing the lowest Nij changed between the two pulses. This showed that material stiffness alone did not explain the full occupant response; the complete stress-strain curve, contact timing, seat geometry, and crash severity also mattered.

- Mass scaling and the relatively coarse foam mesh may have affected response accuracy.
- The material curves were linearly extrapolated beyond approximately 0.6 strain for numerical stability.
- The material inputs did not include strain-rate-dependent behavior.
- The study used one seat geometry and a Hybrid III 50th-percentile male model.
- Individual cases required approximately 24 hours to solve, limiting mesh-refinement and sensitivity studies.

**LS-DYNA explicit dynamics \| LS-PrePost \| foam material modeling and verification \| Hybrid III occupant modeling \| contact analysis \| HIC15 and Nij \| simulation post-processing**

**Public-sharing boundary:** Images and numerical results are taken from my academic course analysis. Source finite element model files are not distributed.

title: Kidney Tissue Classification Using Deep Learning - HLI Summer Research

blocks.text:
**Summer Research Student \| Centre for Heart Lung Innovation, UBC \| Summer 2022**

In summer 2022, I worked with a research team at UBC’s Centre for Heart Lung Innovation to investigate whether kidney tissue images could be used to distinguish diabetic kidney disease (DKD) from healthy tissue. My work focused on the binary classification portion of the project.

The GeoMx Digital Spatial Profiler measures gene expression in selected regions of tissue, but a user still has to identify the regions of interest and the platform does not classify the disease itself. Our team investigated whether convolutional neural networks could use kidney tissue images to distinguish DKD from healthy tissue and predict spatial gene expression.

I used Jupyter on UBC’s Sockeye computing cluster to run a PyTorch workflow using a pretrained AlexNet model. I preprocessed the images by converting and resizing them, generated **256 × 256 pixel patches**, split the image data into training, validation, and test datasets, trained the model, and evaluated how well it distinguished DKD from healthy tissue.

I also collaborated with two other students to present the overall project through a research poster and slide presentation.

The project used **231 pre-selected regions of interest from seven patients: three healthy and four with DKD**. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, true-positive rate, false-positive rate, and ROC AUC.

The binary classification workflow was applied to both GeoMx and H&E kidney tissue images. The comparison considered accuracy, true-positive rate, false-positive rate, and ROC AUC, with similar overall classification accuracy between the two image types. Performance varied across the dataset splits, and with only seven patients, the results were preliminary and not suitable for diagnostic use. A larger patient dataset and comparison of additional CNN architectures would be needed before considering clinical applications.

I worked with two other students to present the project through a poster and slide presentation. My part covered the binary classification work, including the comparison between GeoMx and H&E images. The spatial gene-expression work was completed by the other team members.

For the AUVSI competition, the payload system had to release a rover from at least **30 m**. After landing, the rover needed to drive through obstacles and complete the ground course. The payload team had to balance the release mechanism, component packaging, rover function, and aircraft weight.

As a member of the payload sub-team, I focused on the rover and drop mechanism. I:
- Created the rover wheel, rover assembly, and a motor envelope model used to check component dimensions and spacing.
- Modeled components for a revised payload winch mechanism within the existing payload architecture.
- Prepared CAD models for 3D printing so the team could compare fit and function and select a suitable rover concept.
- Contributed to material and design changes, including repurposing components from earlier concepts, that reduced payload system weight by **50%**.
The team incorporated the CAD into 3D-printed proof-of-concept builds for prototype testing and rover design selection.

The design process produced a rover concept that could be evaluated within the payload system. Material and design changes reduced the payload system weight by **50%**, helping the team manage the aircraft's payload constraints.
